title: Snib and Mottle's Sunstone Mission
markdown:
High in the Hidden Highland of Whispering Peaks, wind sang through rock—old songs, slightly out of tune—and waterfalls came down like silver arguing with gravity. Ancient steps spiralled until they tickled cloud-bellies. Bell-heather clung where a sensible plant would have resigned. Goblin Snib lived there, scruffy, star-eyed, fingers that untangled knots in seconds and sometimes, it must be said, borrowed other people’s shine. He told himself it was research. The shine never believed him.

Mottle, his lizard, wore a thousand emeralds and could vanish into moss like a secret the mountain had decided to keep. On a good day he was a jewel. On a better day he was invisible and still present. Golden eyes: the look of someone who had already understood your next three thoughts and filed the fourth as optional.

A dewy morning, sky blushing as if embarrassed for him, Snib woke so hard acorns left the shelf and a tin cup joined them. Memory arrived second: last night, the Elder’s cave, the stone on its moss like a tame star, the thought I’ll just hold it, then I’ll know how sunrise feels in the hand. The Sunstone—robin-egg, warm, a thousand mornings pulsing—sat on his table looking innocent and stolen. Borrowed, he corrected, for keeping safe, which was a sentence that did not impress mountains. It belonged on the Elder of the Cliff Dwellers’ cushion before first light kissed the highest teeth. Grumpy Elders were a career hazard. So was Lyra, if the news got a soundtrack.

“Emergency,” he whispered, dry-leaf voice. “Back. Now.”

Mottle left a perfect dewdrop mid-journey, tongue-flick: loyalty, the ordinary kind.

Winding steps. Then gold light and a lute with theatrical ambitions. Lyra the Elf Bard stepped from mist as if mist had a stage door: moonlight hair, permanent awe.

“Hark! Brave Snib of the Peaks! Quest to return the stolen Sunstone or twilight tears and darkness forever!”

Snib nearly somersaulted. “Borrowed. For keeping safe. Not a quest. A talking-to, avoided.”

Lyra’s flourish almost sent Mottle off a ledge. “Fate weaves! Legend for all time!”

Snib sighed. Lyra spoke as if the ballad were already printed. “Less story. More delivery.”

Their path, still trying to be speedy, took the wobbly bridge over a chasm that collected echoes for sport. Far below, a river practised being a roar. Sky went purple-orange, the showy hour. Under the boards, clinging to mossy stone like jewellery that had escaped a queen, hundreds of glow-worms made a second sky, green and private, water turned magical by borrowed light. Snib forgot the clock, the Elder, the word borrowed. “Secret stars. Right here.” Mottle nudged the mission back into his hand and still stared, amber gates wide. Even a lizard may pause for wonder without being late, Snib decided, and then decided they were late anyway.

Cleverness, which had been on a break, returned. Speed alone would not beat a bard to a cave; they needed a secret, a cheat the mountain had forgotten to advertise. An old whisper on the wind, the sort Snib collected the way other goblins collected spoons: a dragon on the highest peak, power, secrets older than the stones, possibly a shortcut if you asked without sounding like a legend.

“Ignis,” Snib said, and Mottle was already pointing his nose upslope, which was as good as a vote.

The climb was not for people who liked knees. Steep, then steeper; wind like a lonely ghost with icy fingers and a taste for ears; little smokes from cracks smelling of burnt toast and old secrets. Snib talked to keep his courage employed. Mottle saved his breath for the rock. At last a huge opening, and Ignis filled it: storm-sky scales, a bed of glittering gems that had not applied for the role of mattress, impressive nose-clouds, mysterious on purpose, as if mystery were a hat he refused to take off even in bed.

“Who dares disturb thinking time?” Rumble in the boots, and under it a crumb of interest.

“Snib and Mottle. Sunstone to return. A quick way?”

Slow amber blinks. “Quick ways are earned.” A smoke ring wobbled and vanished, professionally.

“If you’re going to be mysterious, be punctual about it.”

Another blink, geological. “On time. For a dragon. New. Fine. Wind tunnel past the ridge. Windy. Wet. Fast.”

Gap-toothed grin. “Mottle. Dark and slippery. Your sort of map.”

Tail-flick. Hidden paths already tingling the scales.

“Wait,” Ignis boomed, less gravitas. “My story? My smoke rings? How will the world know?”

Snib paused at the ridge. Mottle was already a green comma on stone. “Your wisdom matters. Today we needed his eyes. Partner. He chooses the quiet path, not the loudest.”

A chirp of agreement from height. Scratch behind the head.

“Not just found?”

“He chose me too.”

Respect, rare, crossed the ancient face. They went into swirl.

The tunnel was as advertised: a damp argument that had been going on since geology. Wind shoved; water found their collars; the dark had echoes with opinions. Mottle’s sense drew them—left at a drip that meant false, right at a warmer breath, pause when the floor lied. Snib followed the green flicker of a scale when his own eyes gave up. They came out a small mossy mouth, coughing, grinning the particular grin of people who are wet and not dead. Dawn’s first rose was already on the Elder’s cave, a blush on stone. Shaky fingers, familiar stand, the Sunstone sighed into place as if it had only been out for a walk. Light warm, legal, no longer a pocket problem. Snib sat down hard and counted his remaining acorns, which was none, and did not mind.

Lyra arrived on cue, lute ready for success, and blinked at a job already done. “Behold! Legend!”

Snib’s smile reached the twinkles. He had wanted to put a thing back. Goblin cleverness, a wet tunnel, a lizard who saw what hurry missed. Mottle polished a scale in new sun, pleased. The peaks kept whispering. Nobody needed a sermon about partnership; the stone was home, which was the whole plot.
characters: Snib (goblin Snib), Mottle (lizard Mottle), Ignis (a dragon who is trying very hard to seem mysterious)
audience: children aged 9-10, amusing mountain fantasy adventure for independent readers
author: StoryGen Community
